Model of record: the one-page model summary applied the forecast inputs to the wrong FY2025 revenue base. This memo applies the same inputs to the correct base; the end notes explain the error and define "our base" and "consensus".

Summary: key insights, implications and conclusions

Fevertree has stopped being a growth company that sells tonic and has become a brand-royalty company with a soft-drinks business attached. Since 1-Feb-25 Molson Coors has run Fevertree's United States business under an exclusive licence. The US is 35% of brand revenue and three-quarters of the forecast revenue growth. The licence shares the US profit broadly equally at EBITDA and guarantees Fevertree a minimum royalty for 2026-30 that steps up each year and has not been disclosed (this memo calls it "the floor"). The rest of the group (UK 29% of brand revenue, Europe 26%, Rest of World 10%) earns a 23.6% segment margin, grows about 3% a year and carries about £23m of central costs.

The whole forecast margin recovery comes from the US royalty, and a contract that nobody outside Fevertree and Molson Coors can see sets that royalty. The group EBITDA margin of 11.3% is a third of its 2019 level. Our base case takes the margin to about 15% by FY2028 and consensus takes it to 16.5%; in both, the increase comes from the US royalty line.

The five insights that matter most.

1
The floor, not the profit share, probably sets the US royalty today, so the US sales line that the market watches does not reach Fevertree's earnings. Redburn estimates the US joint operation's 2026 EBITDA margin at 5.4% on about £143m of revenue. That estimate implies a joint-operation profit of £7-8m and a half-share for Fevertree of £3.5-4m for the full year, yet Fevertree booked £4.1m of US royalty in H1 2026 alone. The guarantee is therefore setting the royalty, and Jefferies says so in words: the royalty is "effectively underwritten by the step-changed guarantee". While the floor binds (FY2026 and probably FY2027), a 20% US scanner print adds nothing to EPS and a destocking half subtracts nothing. US revenue is a concentrated driver of the narrative and the multiple, and only a diffuse driver of earnings. No broker has drawn this conclusion.
2
Fevertree's earnings over the next 18 months are more predictable than their drivers suggest, and its share price is less predictable than its earnings. FY2026 EBITDA is settled within about ±£1.5m: glass is 100% hedged, the tariff refunds and the packaging levy are known, the floor binds and two months are left. FY2027 EBITDA sits in a £52-64m range around our £58.3m, and the floor both truncates the downside and absorbs the upside. The share price, by contrast, has traded between 711p and 973p in twelve months with no change to the profit outlook, and 79% of its daily variance is the stock's own news; the beverage basket explains only 21%.
3
Consensus is credible in direction but stretched in two lines in particular, and our base sits 15% below consensus on FY2027 EPS and 20% below on FY2028 EPS. The two large gaps are consensus's US revenue growth and its FY2028 Rest of Group margin, which falls in the year glass-energy hedges drop to 33%. Two smaller gaps complete the difference: consensus has US marketing falling from 20% to 11% of US revenue, and it keeps interest income rising on cash the company is spending on buybacks. The revisions already point toward our base. Beneath an EPS line that buybacks hold flat, consensus EBITDA has fallen 2% and consensus sales 3% over twelve months, while the share of Buy ratings has doubled to 40% on the US story. That combination is the pattern of a consensus that resets slowly, not of one that upgrades.
4
The market underprices both Fevertree's downside protections and its upside caps, and over the next 18 months the caps matter more. Four protections and three caps are absent from broker arguments. The caps dominate for now because our base already sits 15-20% below consensus; the protections matter more once the Molson Coors standstill nears its end in February 2028.
5
At a fair multiple, the shareholder return comes mostly from earnings and dividends, not from re-rating. At 914.5p the shares trade at 24.5x our two-year-forward EPS of about 37p and 19.8x consensus's 46p. That multiple is at the 19th percentile of the stock's five-year range and the 4th percentile of its ten-year range, but 60-100% above beverage peers at 10-15x. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple of 38.8x comes from a ten-year band that includes the 2015-19 company (60% revenue growth, 30-35% EBITDA margins, 40-60x earnings). The relevant range is the last five years (median 25.2x), and the guideline itself says that a stock in a turning-up phase warrants the lower part of its range. At 22-25x on our base, the total return is about +4% to +19% to end-2027 and +27% to +43% to mid-2029 (9-14% a year), with the multiple contributing between −10% and +2%. Consensus earnings at the same multiple give +29% to +46% to end-2027. That bull case needs upgrades that the next 6-12 months are unlikely to produce.

Implication for Richard's test of an unusually positive skew to fundamentals and to upgrades: the skew is not present yet. Over the next 6-12 months the probable path is that the company reports guidance "met on profit, light on revenue, never raised", and that brokers trim FY2027-28 EBITDA consensus by 5-9%.

Five dated events could flip the skew, and three outcomes would flip it. The events are Molson Coors' Q3 call on 5-Nov-26, the January 2027 pre-close trading update, the FY2027 outlook on 30-Mar-27, the April 2027 anniversary of the first US national campaign, and the February 2028 standstill expiry. The outcomes that would turn Fevertree into a live upgrade engine are a disclosed 2027 floor of about £22m or more, a US scanner growth rate held above 15% through the April 2027 anniversary, or a win in the packaging-levy court case. Until then the case is a dated watch-list with a real floor.

1Operating environment: tailwinds, headwinds and risks

The operating environment removes category growth from the forecast, so every point of Fevertree's growth must now come from distribution, share and new occasions. Fevertree's core occasion, gin and tonic, is shrinking structurally: IWSR projects UK gin volumes down 8% a year to 2027, and the UK on-trade is about 35% below its 2019 level. The global mixers market grows about 4.3% a year to 2030 (from $16.4bn to $21.1bn), half its pandemic-inflated 2020-24 rate. Distribution gains are a one-off step with a natural half-life, not a growth rate, so they cannot replace category growth indefinitely.

Three tailwinds are real, and the strongest of them is also the case's single dependency. Brewers are filling their delivery networks with soft drinks: Molson Coors brings 400 distributors, 500,000 accounts and 30,000 daily deliveries, and the "golden case" of premium mixers earns wholesalers three to four times beer's revenue per litre. Moderation favours adult soft drinks: the beyond-tonic range, 47% of group sales, grew 13% in H1 2026, and no- and low-alcohol drinks grow about 7% a year. Costs are unusually well placed through 2027: glass energy is 100% hedged in 2026 and 66% in 2027, aluminium is materially hedged, transatlantic freight is back to normal, carbon dioxide comes from biomass, and US tariffs are gone from H2 2026, with refunds. The first tailwind, the partner's network, is the one on which the whole US case depends.

Competition is easing where Fevertree's growth is and tightening where its profit is. In the US, Q Mixers, one-fifth of Fever-Tree's US size, is contracting by over 20%, and Keurig Dr Pepper took 8% of net price. In the UK and Europe, Carlsberg-Britvic's London Essence, AG Barr's Fentimans and Frobishers, Schweppes campaigns and private label (38-45% of mixers in Spain and the Netherlands) press on the profitable core, and the files show Fevertree's first European value-share loss, about 20 basis points in the four weeks to 4-Oct-26.

The UK consumer weakens into H2 2026, and a premium product sold through bars to spirits drinkers carries more of that squeeze than a staple does. UK inflation is 3.5%, a Bank Rate rise is priced for 5-Nov-26, the energy price cap is forecast to rise about 16% in January and 2027 growth forecasts have been cut to 1.0%. Rates above 5% and a risk-off market that sells small, complex, partner-dependent stocks first are headwinds to the discount rate; Fevertree's net cash passes that market's debt test. The regulatory items are mostly known and mostly small:

Fevertree's cost position is the mirror image of 2022: a relative advantage in 2027, then exposure in 2028. In 2027 peers' input costs rise (Morgan Stanley has Carlsberg's up 5.4%) while two-thirds of Fevertree's glass energy is locked. In 2028 two-thirds is open.

So-what for the forecasts. Model the US as a distribution step that fades to a velocity growth rate, the UK flat, and Europe at low single digits with share at risk. Let hedges help margins through 2027 and run a 2028 cost scenario. Do not extrapolate the UK's +3% in H1 2026, which had good weather and a record off-trade share behind it.

Where we differ from the market

The sell-side names the 2028 hedge roll-off as the key cost risk, but 2027 carries a similar risk per unit of energy. The unhedged third of 2027 faces a higher forward gas price (€80/MWh) than the unhedged two-thirds of 2028 (€49/MWh), and glass makers set most contracts annually over the winter. The market also treats US spirits weakness as the main demand risk, but the real demand risk sits in the UK on-trade and in European share. Keurig Dr Pepper's US refreshment segment grew 10.9% in Q3 with volume and mix up 7.2%, which shows that the premium soft-drink occasion in the US is healthy.

Strongest counter-case. US spirits value including ready-to-drink turned positive (+3%) in October after −4.6% in September. If the US spirits malaise is cyclical and the dollar strengthens into 2027, as Morgan Stanley expects, a dollar-denominated royalty and a recovering core occasion would make the environment a net tailwind.

What would change my view. Two consecutive twelve-week European share gains; UK on-trade data stabilising through the winter; calendar-2027 gas forwards below €60/MWh.

Conclusion: the environment neither carries nor sinks the case. Headwinds slightly outweigh tailwinds, category growth is absent, cost visibility is excellent for 2027 and poor for 2028, and the strongest tailwind sits inside a partner.
Score 45Score: 44, set by the Rater. The core occasion is shrinking (UK gin -8% a year, UK on-trade a third below 2019, US premium spirits down), mixers grow only about 4% a year, the UK consumer weakens, glass taxes and private label and rival premium launches bite in Europe (first European share loss), against real tailwinds in moderation and adult soft drinks (beyond-tonic +13%), brewers pushing soft drinks through their networks, US tariffs removed and a benign 2027 input market that turns in 2028; net slightly negative and the forecast's growth comes from distribution, not the category. I sit just below the External change forces group's 45 and just above Carlsberg, whose mature beer offset by soft drinks is the closest picture, with no regained pricing to lift it as at CVS.

2Internally-driven corporate change

Corporate change is the strongest group in the case: in two years Fevertree has rebuilt its earnings model rather than adjusted it. The direct US subsidiary (about 85 people, with its own inventory, receivables, transatlantic freight and tariffs) became an exclusive licence. Under the licence Molson Coors produces, sells, funds working capital and overheads, pays for a doubled marketing budget (including the first US national campaign, from April 2026) and guarantees a minimum royalty for 2026-30. Fevertree sold Fevertree USA for $25.4m with no gain or loss, and Molson Coors paid £71m for an 8.5% stake.

Four further changes reinforce the rebuild.

  • The portfolio has moved from mixers to a multi-occasion adult soft-drink platform. Five flavour platforms are half of sales and produced 85% of H1 2026 growth; non-alcoholic ready-to-drink cans sell at £1.90 in over 4,000 UK outlets; draught volumes rose 185% in trial and are rolling out across managed pub estates; ginger beer grew 20%.
  • Capital allocation has turned to shareholder returns. Fevertree bought back £100m of shares in 2025 and £60m in 2026, at 16-20 times forward earnings.
  • Operations have hardened. Hedging now extends to 2028 after the company was caught short in 2022; working capital fell from 28.5% of revenue (2023) to 16.7% (2025); an enterprise systems programme is under way; two continental co-packers were reinstated.
  • Governance has improved. Remuneration was reformed in 2026 toward financial delivery; 75% of the board is independent, chaired by a former SABMiller finance chief; the Chair bought 44,674 shares at 780p on 11-Sep-26.

Three qualifications carry through into the forecasts. First, the 2025 net cash return to shareholders was £29.3m, not £100m: the buyback mostly recycled Molson Coors' share subscription, new shares were issued at about 655p and bought back at 750-850p, and basic shares fell only about 1%. Second, a partner under strain executes the change. Molson Coors has a new chief executive (Rahul Goyal), its Americas volumes fell 4.8% in H1 2026 and its scanned consumption fell 6% in Q3; it is running a $450m cost programme, has cut 400 salaried roles, and has bought Monaco, a $275m ready-to-drink business that competes for the same sales calls. Third, Fevertree's margin plan and its growth plan both rely on the same marketing money.

What is absent is as telling as what has changed. The founder has run the company for 22 years with no groomed successor, and the company's own risk register names his loss as severely disruptive. There has been no guidance raise since 2022, no real price increase and no acquisition. The US capability inside Fevertree (the North America chief executive, the distribution director and the team) has gone without replacement. Central costs still rise (+7% in 2025), exceptional costs have been about £5m a year for three years running, and the 2025 bonus paid out near maximum while adjusted EBITDA fell 16%.

The corporate change is broad, strong and already executed, but the partner resources it and an undisclosed contract transmits it to Fevertree's earnings. The licence has converted "heroic hustle" into mechanical distribution, which is the pattern that made Monster successful after it moved to Coca-Cola's network. It also carries two risks from other partner-distributed brands: the Celsius risk of pipeline fill followed by destocking, and the Snapple risk that a specialist on-premise heartland is diluted by a mass network whose beer sales representatives lack mixology skills.

So-what: the earnings function has changed. Fevertree's group EBITDA used to be volume times margin. It is now the larger of the floor and about half the US joint operation's EBITDA, plus a Rest of Group profit that barely moves, less central costs. That change is why Fevertree's profit is predictable while its narrative is not.

Where we differ from the market

The buy-side credits the £160m of gross buybacks as a strong capital-return story, but net of the share subscription and of interest income forgone, the balance sheet adds only about 1-2% a year to EPS. The sell-side treats the free-cash-flow floor of "at least £100m" over 2027-28 as conservative (Jefferies, because consensus free cash flow is £117.6m); we read it as realistic. Our base reaches it at EBITDA 12% below consensus, through the working-capital release.

Strongest counter-case. The partner's own weakness is Fevertree's strength. A brewer with falling beer volumes has every incentive to push the one brand in its portfolio growing 16%, and 60% of Molson Coors' distributors expect Fever-Tree to gain share, second only to Coors Banquet.

What would change my view. Disclosure of the royalty schedule; a named successor or a strengthened executive bench; central costs falling as a share of revenue in FY2026; Molson Coors confirming on 5-Nov-26 that its 2027 incentives are tied to Fevertree volume.

Conclusion: the internal change forces are strong and already in place, scoring well on strategy, perimeter, portfolio and capital allocation. But they are borrowed from a partner, undisclosed in how they reach earnings, and unaccompanied by the leadership, guidance or pricing changes that would make them self-sustaining.
Score 67Score: 68, set by the Rater. A large strategic move already executed and reaching earnings: the US subsidiary replaced by an exclusive Molson Coors licence with a guaranteed, stepping-up minimum royalty (US EBITDA £8.2m to about £27m by FY2028, the main source of the forecast EPS growth), a multi-occasion portfolio that produced 85% of H1 2026 growth, £160m of buybacks, hedging and working-capital discipline, and pay reformed toward financial delivery. Held below the 75 band because it is resourced by a partner in its own upheaval, transmits through an undisclosed contract, and comes with no price rise, no guidance raise and central and exceptional costs still rising; slightly above the group's 65 because a pivot of this size, already booked in the royalty line, is a large change force.

3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Fevertree leads a concentrated premium-mixer tier that is consolidating toward it. Fevertree is seven times the size of its next premium rival and has been the top-selling and top-trending mixer in the world's best bars for eleven years. Retailers restrict shelf space to high-velocity leaders, distributors carry the brand with the best revenue per case, and the Molson Coors network now locks craft challengers out of the top US wholesalers.

27%US tonic, value share, number one
32%US ginger beer, value share, number one
~90%of US premium mixers, with Q Mixers
>⅔of European premium mixers
44%of UK on-trade mixers
21.6%of UK tonic

The industry structure is fragile at three edges. Schweppes, Canada Dry and private label set the price umbrella, and 10-15% of premium-mixer buyers are "stretch" customers who trade down. UK consolidators (Coca-Cola Europacific Partners and Carlsberg-Britvic hold about 40% of UK retail soft-drink volume) can bundle beer and soft drinks in negotiations and in chiller space. And the US route to market is one partner.

Fevertree's moat protects volume and share far better than it protects Fevertree's own margin, because the brand deliberately shares its rent with the trade. Gross margin is 33-37%, against 55% in 2016.

  • The customer moat is real. Bartender advocacy turns into placement through venue economics: venues earn a 75% gross margin on the product and a 33% higher cash margin than on mainstream mixers. 3.6m UK households buy the brand, half of them beyond tonic, which raises the cost to a retailer of delisting it.
  • The distribution moat is widening, by Molson Coors' 500,000 US accounts.
  • There is no production moat. Outsourced co-packing is 32% of cost of goods, glass 24% and logistics 19%.
  • The regulatory position is negative. Glass taxes fall on the vast majority of Fevertree's volume, against about 2% of Coca-Cola Europacific Partners'.
  • Pricing power is latent, not demonstrated. Fevertree took no price rises in the 2022-23 inflation and a 300 basis point catch-up in 2024; European price and mix rose 1.6% over 52 weeks; US tracked value grows slower than volume as eight-pack cans grow; and a competitor describes Fevertree's drinks as "becoming cheaper" relative to its own.

The financial profile is capital-light and debt-free, but its outputs are mediocre for the category. Capex is about 1% of sales, and Molson Coors funds US working capital, overheads and production capex. The balance sheet has £3.8m of leases and no pension. Returns on tangible capital are far above 30%, and returns on operating capital recover from about 21% (FY2026) to about 32% (FY2028) on consensus. Yet the EBITDA margin of 11.3% is the lowest among beverage peers (chart below), the EBIT margin of 9% compares with a sector range of 12-15%, and add-backs make up a fifth of earnings: normalised EPS was 24.1p against reported EPS of 18.8p in FY2025, mostly because of recurring "one-off" restructuring and the Molson Coors deal costs.

The forecast fixes the volatility of free cash flow more than its level. Free cash flow swung from −£4.5m in FY2023 to £70.1m in FY2024 on inventory movements; our base has it steady at about £50m a year from FY2027.

Management is a proven brand-builder and decisive strategist, but a weak forecaster and operator. The company is founder-led: Tim Warrillow has been chief executive since 2004 and holds about 5% without selling, and Andy Branchflower has been finance director since 2013. Judged by actions, they built a £23m business into a £375m category leader, closed the Molson Coors licence in weeks, hedged after 2022 and bought back shares at the bottom of the range. Judged by numbers, the record since 2022 is four misses and no raise (topic 4), and the 2019-23 margin decline was more than 500 basis points worse than the peer median. Planning runs on spreadsheets, decisions funnel through the founder, the bench is thin, and investor relations has been run on an interim basis since mid-2025.

Pay discipline is the governance blemish. Base pay rose 28% and 35% for the two executives in 2024, during margin compression. The long-term incentive was 70% weighted to revenue, so it paid for the top line the thesis needs and insulated executives from the margin the thesis also needs; it was reformed in 2026. Management's ambition is the most growth-led in the peer set ("double-digit" US growth and a US business five times its historical size), and it is delegated to a partner whose priority is beer.

Fevertree is a high-quality brand inside a medium-quality company. The brand's advantage justifies modelling continued US share gains and a price held at its premium. It does not justify price rises above inflation or margins returning toward their 2016-19 level. Weight management's forward statements lightly, lean profit forecasts to the lower half of broker ranges, and treat the founder's continued presence and the remuneration reform as necessary conditions rather than as upside.

Where we differ from the market

The Buy case treats Fevertree as a high-quality compounder whose margin costs temporarily crushed; the industry structure says the 2016-19 margin was the anomaly. The margin was always going to be shared with the channel, and the US model of a floor plus a half-share caps the group margin near 17% (Deutsche Bank's ceiling under the profit share) however well the US goes.

Strongest counter-case. Returns on new US capital are almost unbounded because no capital is needed, the Rest of Group's 23.6% segment margin is genuinely good, and a brand chosen by top bars for eleven years and bought by 3.6m UK households is a scarcer asset than its 11% group margin implies. A bidder (the obvious one already holds 9.4%) would pay for the brand, not the margin.

What would change my view. A net UK or European price rise above inflation in 2027 without share loss; central costs below 5.5% of revenue; a Rest of Group margin above 25% in a year with unhedged energy.

Conclusion: the industry structure and the brand genuinely support the case (a concentrated premium tier consolidating toward Fevertree, and channel loyalty that Fevertree pays for). But the business model shares its rent with the trade, the financial profile is capital-light yet low-margin and heavy in add-backs, and management is strong on brand and strategy and weak on delivery, bench and pay discipline.
Score 54Score: 54, set by the Rater. Qualitatively a leader of a concentrated premium tier consolidating toward it, with a real customer and distribution moat and almost unbounded returns on new US capital, but no production moat, pricing power latent rather than shown, rent shared by design with the trade and one partner, and management strong on brand and strategy but weak on delivery, bench and pay. The figures agree once read correctly: EBITDA margin 11.3% (24th percentile) and a fifth of earnings in add-backs against capital-light, net-cash returns (ROIC 9.4%, 64th percentile), and the 2019-23 margin collapse from 29.6% to 8.4% makes predictability ordinary; coherent with the groups (62, 60, 50, 46), level with Vodafone and above Munters.

4Guidance: conservatism, expectations management, delivery record

Fevertree's guidance is honest, minimal and set at consensus, so it holds no sandbag to release. FY2026 guidance (brand revenue £402.4m, adjusted EBITDA £49.9m, reaffirmed on 10-Sep-26) equals consensus because the company guides by endorsing the consensus it compiles. There is no FY2027 revenue or EBITDA guidance and no margin target; the 15% margin target was withdrawn in Q2 2024. The only forward numbers are "at least £100m" of free cash flow across 2027-28 (consensus about £118m) and "double-digit" US growth over the medium term (consensus +18% and +16% for FY2027-28).

From 2022 to 2026 the record contains no guidance raise. Jefferies calls Fevertree an "honest tracker" after four years of misses, the opposite archetype to Carlsberg, which has beaten its initial EBIT guidance by 300-870 basis points in almost every year since 2016, and to AG Barr, which lands in line or slightly ahead.

The material information sits outside the company's guidance. The floor is secret, and Molson Coors' quarterly calls have become a second disclosure channel; Bernstein is pressing Molson Coors' chief executive for partnership metrics.

We expect FY2026 EBITDA guidance to be met and revenue to come in about 1% light. FY2026 needs H2 revenue growth of about 7% and adjusted EBITDA growth of about 24%. Three things help the EBITDA step: an H2 2025 base depressed by the levy provision, about £3.5m of one-off tariff refunds, and a binding floor. We therefore expect EBITDA to be met within about £1m (65% probability). Revenue needs US H2 growth near 20% against a 16% scanner rate, and US shipments already ran slightly ahead of tracked consumer takeaway in H1, so we expect revenue to be about 1% light (55%). The company will report "revenue slightly below, EBITDA in line" as guidance met.

The FY2027 outlook on 30-Mar-27 will more likely rest on the cash floor, "double-digit" US growth and margin "progression" than on an EBITDA figure above consensus. We put a raise at 10% per event, and an endorsement of a consensus that has drifted to £58-62m at 50%.

So-what. Anchor FY2026 on guidance and do not assume a 2027 raise. Expect disappointment to appear as a company-compiled consensus drifting down before the company speaks. That mechanism is slower and less violent than a guidance cut, and the twelve-month revision pattern already shows it.

Where we differ from the market

The Buy-rated brokers read the £100m cash floor as conservative; on our bridge it is realistic. We reach £99-102m at EBITDA 12% below consensus, because working capital unwinds as US goods stop being recharged at cost. No broker has stated that a US print below 12% in January, with EBITDA still near £49.9m, would itself be evidence that the floor binds.

Strongest counter-case. The floor gives management a profit minimum it has never had. A company that knows its 2027 US profit to the pound, and has a pipeline of dated cost savings (tariffs gone, cans localised, refunds), could choose to guide FY2027 explicitly for the first time, and "at least £100m" could be the first of a series of conservative floors.

What would change my view. An FY2027 EBITDA figure in the 30-Mar-27 outlook; disclosure of the royalty schedule; a capital markets day.

Conclusion: guidance is honest and at consensus, from a management with no record of raising, and the only forward number (the cash floor) is realistic rather than conservative. The guidance lens therefore offers no hidden upside, and a slow drift in consensus is the likely mechanism for disappointment.
Score 34Score: 33, set by the Rater. No guidance raise since 2022: FY2022 cut twice, FY2023 15% below the range, the 15% margin target withdrawn in 2024 with revenue +1% against a +10% ambition, FY2025 £2m below company-compiled consensus, H1 2026 only in line; current guidance equals the consensus the company compiles, FY2027 is unguided, and the only forward number (the £100m cash floor) is realistic rather than conservative. A weak two-to-three-year record with no sandbag, near the Guidance group's 36 and just above Solid State.

5Operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Cost leverage is the leverage that matters at Fevertree; volume leverage is small and the US reaches earnings only at a half-share. A 1% move in cost of goods is worth about £2.2m of EBITDA (4.4% of FY2026 EBITDA), and a 10% move in the glass price about £5m (10%). History shows the scale: in 2024 the EBITDA margin rose 530 basis points on revenue up 1%, and from 2019 to 2023 it fell from 29.6% to 8.4% while revenue rose 40%.

Classic fixed-cost leverage is small. Cost of goods is about 60% of Rest of Group revenue and almost entirely variable; the fixed items are central costs (£23.2m and rising), part of marketing, and a small depreciation and amortisation charge. Incremental UK and European revenue therefore drops through at about 30-35%, against an average margin of 23.6%, a leverage ratio of about 1.4x: 1% of Rest of Group revenue (about £2.5m) moves EBITDA by about £0.8m. US revenue reaches Fevertree at about half of the joint operation's incremental EBITDA, roughly 15-20p per pound of US brand revenue, and not at all while the floor binds.

Cost-out of about £10-12m reaches Fevertree's EBITDA by FY2028; it is real and contractually underpinned, but the partner executes all of it. About £5-6m of it is in place by FY2027. None of it comes from Fevertree's own cost base, whose central costs we grow at 2.5% a year. Can localisation is worth about £2.5-3m from 2027, and because the floor is sized to full localisation, the slip in glass localisation is Molson Coors' cost, not Fevertree's.

Financial leverage is nil, and buybacks add only about 1-2% a year to EPS once forgone interest is counted. Fevertree has net cash and £3.8m of leases. Buybacks of about £30m a year from 2027 retire shares at an earnings yield of 3.5% (33p of EPS at 950p), against post-tax interest of 2.8% at a 3.75% cash rate.

One reinforcing loop drives the forecasts, and three balancing loops act on the very lines consensus needs to expand. The reinforcing loop runs from US distribution breadth to velocity, to shelf space, to distributor priority; it is strong now, but saturating as points of distribution fill and as Molson Coors' 2026 incentive on Fevertree volume comes up for renewal. The balancing loops are marketing normalisation against velocity, pipeline fill followed by destocking, and buybacks against lost interest income. The guarantee breaks one loop: it removes the destructive partner loop (less volume, less profit, less push) from Fevertree's profit and loss account until 2030, and it also means that US volume above the floor accrues to Fevertree at only half the joint operation's margin.

Inference: the forecast profit growth is a contractual and cost-removal recovery at the US partner, not operating leverage on volume. EPS grows about 18% a year to FY2028 on 6% revenue growth. Where leverage is high (input costs), it works in both directions, and FY2028 is the year it can reverse.

So-what. The US revenue line is a weak earnings driver and a strong multiple driver. The Rest of Group margin and the royalty step are the earnings drivers. The balance sheet contributes about +1-2% a year to EPS, not the 3-4% that the headline buyback implies.

Where we differ from the market

Consensus counts Fevertree's cash twice, which is worth about 1.5-2p of EPS (4-5%). Consensus has pre-tax profit exceeding EBIT by £2.7m in FY2027 and £3.9m in FY2028, so it keeps the interest income on the cash, while its implied share count falls to 104-107m, so it also spends the cash on buybacks. The market also reads the £160m of gross buybacks as accretion; once interest income forgone is set against the smaller share count, the net gain to EPS is about 2% between FY2025 and FY2028.

Strongest counter-case. If velocity holds as marketing falls (Jefferies' "self-sustaining threshold"), the marketing loop turns reinforcing and the joint operation's margin reaches Redburn's 30% by 2028. The profit share would then rise above the floor and give Fevertree real US operating leverage for the first time; the venue cash-margin mechanism and US glass procurement through O-I Glass would add to it.

What would change my view. Evidence that the joint operation's EBITDA exceeds the floor in 2027 (a royalty above about £22m with marketing still at 20%); a 2027 glass contract priced below 2026's; a US price rise agreed through the joint governance committee.

Conclusion: operating leverage on volume is modest and capped by the partner arrangement, cost leverage is high and two-sided, and there is no financial leverage. Cost-out of £10-12m is real but executed by the partner, and the feedback loops that matter are balancing loops on the very lines consensus needs to expand.
Score 42Score: 42, set by the Rater. Structurally little gearing: Rest of Group cost of goods (about 60% of revenue) is almost all variable and incremental UK and European revenue drops through at only about 1.4 times the average margin, US volume reaches Fevertree at about half the joint operation's margin and not at all while the floor binds, real price rises have not been taken, and there is no financial leverage; buybacks add only 1-2% a year net of lost interest. Lifted off the 25 level by real, contracted cost-out of about £10-12m at the partner by FY2028 and one reinforcing US distribution loop; the forecast 18%-a-year EPS on 6% revenue is a contractual royalty step, not operating leverage, so it does not lift the number.

6Forecast financials: scope for double-digit growth and for higher growth or margins than the past

Our base has EPS compounding about 18% a year to FY2028 on revenue growth of about 6%, and sits 8-20% below consensus EPS from FY2026 to FY2028.

EPS can grow at double digits to FY2028, about 18% a year compound, but from a base that is both depressed and flattered by interest income. The growth breaks down into multiplicative legs: revenue about +6%, margin (EBITDA growth beyond revenue) about +10%, depreciation, amortisation and share-based payment growing more slowly than EBITDA about +2.5%, falling interest income about −4.5%, and a falling share count about +3.3%. The interest and share-count legs nearly cancel. After FY2028, EPS growth falls to about 10% a year, made up of revenue growth plus buybacks.

Revenue cannot grow at double digits: our base has about 6% a year, the same rate as FY2019-25 (6.3%). The US provides about 60% of the increase. The UK is flat to +1%, as tonic declines about 3% a year and beyond-tonic offsets it; Europe grows 3-3.5% and Rest of World 7-8%. Free cash flow becomes steady at about £50m a year (chart in topic 3), helped by a working-capital release of about £12m over 2027-28 as the US goods that Fevertree recharges at cost shrink: statutory US revenue falls from £128m to about £29m by 2028 on Redburn's path.

The margin can rise above its 2023-25 level of 8-11%, but not back to its 2016-19 level of 30-35%, and the whole rise comes from the US royalty. Our base reaches 15% by FY2028: the royalty adds 3.8 points, central costs 0.6 points, and Rest of Group mix subtracts 0.8 points, because the Rest of Group's own margin rises from 23.6% to 24.3% while its share of revenue falls from 65% to 60%. No forecast returns the margin to 2016-19 levels; Deutsche Bank's ceiling under the profit share is about 17%.

Consensus's 16.5% margin in FY2028 needs a Rest of Group margin of roughly 26-27% in the year hedges roll off, which has no precedent in the company's last six years. Our back-solve: consensus EBITDA of £77.5m, less a US line of £29-31m, plus about £25m of central costs, leaves £71-73m of Rest of Group EBITDA on £268m of Rest of Group revenue. Consensus also needs a US royalty near £30m. We hold the Rest of Group margin flat at 24.3% in FY2028, because glass-energy hedges fall to 33% with spot gas above €100/MWh; it rises to 25.2% by FY2030 as prices catch up with costs on a 12-18 month lag.

The range of EPS outcomes widens about threefold from FY2026 to FY2027 and fourfold to FY2028; it is roughly symmetric around our base and skewed down around consensus. FY2026 EPS is 24.5-27.5p, a narrow range. For FY2027 the bear case is 27-28p (US +6% after a destocking half, the floor binding, a Rest of Group margin of 23.5%), our base is 33.0p and the bull case is about 39p (US +17%, early marketing normalisation, the levy won); consensus at 38.9p sits at the bull case. For FY2028 the bear case is about 28p (an energy-cost repeat and the levy lost), our base 39.3p and the bull case about 48p; consensus at 49.4p sits just above the bull case.

Where we differ from the market

The whole gap between our base and consensus sits in two main lines and two smaller ones. The main lines are US revenue growth (our +12% and +10% for FY2027-28, against consensus's +18% and +16%, worth about £4m of EBITDA at Fevertree's half-share and nothing while the floor binds) and the FY2028 Rest of Group margin (£5-7m). US marketing (£2-3m) and interest income (1.5-2p of EPS) make up the rest. We agree with consensus on the UK, Europe, Rest of World, tax and dividends.

Strongest counter-case. The brokers closest to the floor's arithmetic may know that the royalty schedule steps up faster than our £20m (FY2027) and £27m (FY2028). Deutsche Bank has about £29m of US EBITDA by FY2028, and Redburn raised its 2027-28 EPS by 4-6% in September on "better-modelled guaranteed EBITDA". If the 2027 step is £24m and the 2028 step £30m, our FY2027 and FY2028 EPS rise by about 2.8p and 2.1p, and the gap to consensus halves.

What would change my view. The FY2026 segment disclosure on 30-Mar-27 (royalty EBITDA above about £8.5m for H2 2026 would imply a higher floor); a 2027 glass contract; the first scanner print after the April 2027 campaign anniversary.

Conclusion: the forecasts describe a real but borrowed recovery. EPS compounds about 18% a year to FY2028 on 6% revenue growth, and the margin recovers to half its pre-2020 level, almost entirely through a royalty set by a contract we cannot see. Our base sits 15-20% below consensus in FY2027-28, and the gap is concentrated in US revenue and the FY2028 Rest of Group margin.

The events in the window are the Molson Coors Q3 call (5-Nov-26), the January 2027 pre-close, the FY2026 results with the first FY2027 outlook (30-Mar-27), the annual general meeting statement (June 2027) and the H1 2027 results (September 2027); the levy ruling is undated.

Brokers have already added buybacks and kept interest income in their EPS while trimming US revenue and the FY2027 margin, so a flat EPS line hides falling operating lines.

After 30-Mar-27 we expect a further 3-5% cut if the company frames its outlook around cash and momentum and confirms elevated 2027 marketing. The first FY2028 cuts follow as the marketing step is pushed out and Redburn's assumption of zero freight cost in 2028 is corrected for the glass slip. September 2027 then depends on the post-anniversary scanner prints.

Five things could produce upgrades, and we put each at about 10% per event because each would have to coincide with a management that has never raised a number.

The sell-side knows the structure of the case thoroughly but has not done the arithmetic that connects it to the 2027-28 profit line. None has connected a binding floor, a spent cash pile and a 2027 glass contract to the 2027-28 profit line. The items the market has not noticed divide into downside protections (the floor covers the glass slip, the cash floor is realistic, the sugar threshold is a non-issue, the standstill is a bid option) and upside caps (the floor absorbs US upside, consensus EPS carries 2-4% of below-the-line downside, and energy is a risk in 2027 as well as 2028). Because our base sits 15-20% below consensus, the unnoticed caps outweigh the unnoticed protections for the next 6-12 months. Beyond that horizon, the standstill expiry (around February 2028) and any disclosure of the floor could turn the narrative gap in Fevertree's favour.

9Riskiness and simplicity of forecasts and expectations

The case is simple to monitor and hard to forecast, because the largest driver is a contract that nobody outside the two companies can see. The diffuse items (UK, Europe and Rest of World revenue, tax, buybacks) are close to consensus and low-variance.

Four numbers decide which case the next 18 months validate:

  1. the FY2027 royalty step, which is undisclosed;
  2. the FY2027-28 Rest of Group margin, which depends on glass energy;
  3. the US scanner growth rate after the April 2027 campaign anniversary;
  4. the packaging-levy ruling.

Consensus needs, on top of everything our base needs, three levers that the company has never shown working together, all in FY2028. Our base needs the partner to keep executing (cushioned at EBITDA by the floor, though not at revenue), hedges to hold in 2027, and a Monster-type fade in US growth rather than a Celsius-type destock. Consensus also needs a marketing cut without velocity loss, sustained US growth two to three years after a distribution step, and a Rest of Group margin rise in an unhedged year. The Rest of Group margin has no precedent of rising in that way: it fell with scale from 2019 to 2023 and rose only when costs fell.

The demand side can be tracked monthly and the profit side only half-yearly. Circana scanner data arrives monthly but covers only 35-40% of US sales and none of the 250,000 US on-trade accounts; Nielsen Europe arrives every four weeks, Molson Coors reports quarterly and Fevertree half-yearly. The share price has swung 25-30% in a year without fundamental change, and 79% of its daily variance is the stock's own news.

Sudden, high-magnitude fundamental risks are concentrated in one partner, one person, one cost line and one data series, and the floor cushions earnings but not the multiple. Perception risks come from read-across: spirits results, Molson Coors' beer volumes, ready-to-drink and GLP-1 weight-loss-drug headlines, and UK hospitality data.

Fevertree's own history is the relevant precedent, and it says that re-ratings in this stock have needed earnings upgrades, not mere stabilisation. Beverages are low-cyclical, but the market prices Fevertree as a premium growth stock, not a staple. The stock was a growth darling at 45-60x and de-rated to about 20x as margins collapsed in 2022-23 on costs, not demand, while guidance was missed repeatedly. Precedents for partner-distributed brands point both ways: Monster compounded; Celsius destocked in 2024; Snapple collapsed after Quaker moved it into mass distribution; BodyArmor lost 10% of volume under Coca-Cola.

The bear and bull outcomes are symmetric in price, but the probability-weighted skew is down, because the bull case needs consensus earnings while the bear case needs only a cost year. On unchanged earnings, a fair trough multiple takes the shares to 760p (18.6x, the five-year 10th percentile, on about 41p of two-year-forward EPS at end-2027). The bear case (16x on about 36p after a cost year and a destocking half) is about 580p (−37%); brokers' bear anchors are Morgan Stanley's 570p and Jefferies' stress case of 400p. The bull case (25x on consensus's 50p) is about 1,250p (+37%).

Where we differ from the market

The market treats US revenue as the main risk to earnings; it is the main risk to the multiple and almost no risk to EBITDA while the floor binds. The market treats 2028 as the cost-risk year; 2027 carries a third of glass energy unhedged at a higher forward gas price.

Strongest counter-case. The risk profile is more cushioned than at any point in the company's listed history: a contractual US floor to 2030, two-thirds of 2027 glass energy hedged, tariffs gone, net cash, a working-capital release, and no debt in a market where interest cost is the new drag on European earnings. An EBITDA collapse like 2022-23 is very unlikely before FY2028.

What would change my view. Disclosure of the floor, which would collapse the forecast error around the largest driver; a 2027 glass price; the first scanner print after the April 2027 anniversary.

Conclusion: the case is simple to monitor and hard to forecast. Risk is concentrated in one undisclosed contract, one commodity, one partner's budget and one founder. The floor and hedges cushion it at the EBITDA line through 2027, but nothing cushions the multiple: a small, partner-dependent growth stock in a risk-off market can fall 25-35% on evidence that the US acceleration was a one-off step rather than a lasting growth rate.

10Lifecycle: where the stock plausibly is

The stock is turning up, but the phase is not yet reinforcing, because the reinforcing phase needs an upgrade cycle that the next 6-12 months are unlikely to deliver. The Master Dashboard's rule places the stock in "Turning/Inflecting", and the components support that reading:

  • Operating-line revisions are negative beneath a flat EPS line, and the Buy share has doubled ahead of the estimates.
  • The narrative has pivoted to a US engine whose profit contribution is contractual for the next year or more.

  • The price has made a higher low (711p in March 2026 against 674p in December 2024) and sits 8.6% above a 200-day average that has risen in 7 of 12 months.
  • Management's record is of cutting and missing, never raising.
  • The internal change (licence, floor, buybacks, hedges) is executed and visible in the operating metrics, but not yet in estimates.

The bottoming phase of 2024-25 is behind the stock. That phase brought the margin collapse, the strategic reset, the licence announcement and estimates rebased by 35-40%. The thesis-broadening step, from "the floor protects us" to "the profit share exceeds the floor", is dated to 2028 on Redburn's own 30% joint-operation margin, and later if marketing normalises more slowly. The stalling risk is specific and dated: the April 2027 campaign anniversary and the September 2027 interim results, with a destocking half as the mechanism.

So-what: time the stock around dated events rather than hold it through them. A turning-up stock with a company-specific multiple at the bottom of its range and a probable consensus reset ahead rewards timing. The events that could move it from turning up to reinforcing are the FY2027 outlook (30-Mar-27), the scanner prints after the campaign anniversary (May-July 2027) and the standstill expiry (February 2028).

Where we differ from the market

The Buy-rated brokers describe the stock as already reinforcing ("US starting to accelerate", a top pick); the revision data and the binding floor say the reinforcement is in sell-out, not in earnings. The estimates have not turned.

Strongest counter-case. Lifecycle phases are identified only in hindsight. A stock whose US scanner growth rate has tripled in nine months, whose partner's distributors expect share gains and whose multiple sits at a decade low may already be in the reinforcing phase for the component that leads (demand), with estimates to follow within two prints.

What would change my view. Positive FY2027 EBITDA revisions after January; a company endorsement of £63m or more of FY2027 EBITDA on 30-Mar-27; a scanner growth rate above 15% after April 2027.

Conclusion: the stock is turning up. The bottoming is done, the reinforcing phase depends on an upgrade cycle that the next 6-12 months are unlikely to deliver, and the stalling risk is dated to the April 2027 campaign anniversary.

11The fair multiple

The fair multiple for this phase is 22-25x two-year-forward EPS on our base, drawn from the stock's last five years, not the 38.8x guideline drawn from ten. Viewforth's guideline for the Turning/Inflecting phase is 38.8x two-year-forward EPS, the 60th percentile of the stock's ten-year history and 113% above the 18.2x on the Master Dashboard today.

The ten-year band is the wrong reference for this phase and this company, because 2015-19 dominates it. In 2015-19 Fevertree compounded revenue at about 60% a year on a 30-35% EBITDA margin and traded at 40-60x. The business now grows 6% a year at a 12-15% margin, depends on a partner for its growth engine, and has a margin ceiling near 17% under the profit share. The relevant ranges are the last five years and the last two:

Three further pieces of evidence point to the lower part of the range. First, the guideline itself says that a turning-up stock, whose forecasts are more uncertain, warrants the lower part of its range; even inside the ten-year band, the lower part is the 10th percentile at 21.6x, not the 60th. Second, beverage peers trade at 10-15x at their own decade lows and global staples at about 17x, and Fevertree's premium is paid for its growth story and a floored royalty, not for its sector. Third, the multiple is company-specific (79% of daily variance is the stock's own news), so a sector re-rating would carry it only partly (beta 0.68).

The 22-25x range runs from the two-year median to the five-year median, and holds while the floor is undisclosed and the FY2027 outlook unknown. The range sits just above the five-year 10th percentile (18.6x) and the ten-year 10th percentile (21.6x). It rises toward 28-30x only on evidence of earnings upgrades, because re-ratings in this stock have needed upgrades, not stabilisation (topic 9).

The market is paying our fair multiple for our earnings and a discount for consensus's earnings, which is the right way round if consensus is going to be cut. Today's 914.5p is 24.5x our two-year-forward EPS of about 37p, inside the fair range, and 19.8x consensus's 46p, below it.

Where we differ from the market

No broker values the stock against its own recent range. Redburn anchors on calendar-year P/E against spirits groups (a premium of over 100%), and Jefferies on growth-adjusted comparisons with global staples (29.8x against 17x, justified by growth and the floor). We agree with Deutsche Bank that the multiple would amplify a 10% earnings downgrade.

Strongest counter-case. If the floor is disclosed near £25-30m a year for 2028 and the profit share is seen to exceed it, the stock becomes a royalty company with a 15-17% margin, 10% EPS growth and a bid option. Brand-royalty assets have traded at 25-30x, and the ten-year band's lower quartile (about 28-30x) would then be defensible.

What would change my view. Two consecutive upgrade events; disclosure of the royalty schedule; a sector re-rating with estimate support.

Conclusion: the fair multiple for this phase is 22-25x two-year-forward EPS on our base, drawn from the stock's last five years rather than from a ten-year band that describes a different company. The 38.8x guideline would be reachable only in a peak-delivery phase with upgrades in hand, and today's 24.5x on our base sits inside the fair range.
Score 78Score: 80, set by the Rater. Both raw readings are cheap, which would give A, but most of the own-range cheapness is deserved: the ten-year range belongs to the 2015-19 company (60% growth, 30-35% margins), and on the memo's base EPS, 15-20% below consensus, 24.5x sits at the five-year median and inside the memo's 22-25x fair range, so that measure reads neutral and I move the letter to B. The cohort discount to its own norm is still large even after the growth gap narrowed (and it trades 60-100% above beverage peers), so it stays cheap and I place it mid-band.

12Total shareholder return, split into earnings, multiple and dividends

On our base at a 22-25x fair multiple, the total return is about +4% to +19% to end-2027 and +27% to +43% to mid-2029, and it comes from earnings and dividends with the multiple roughly flat. The starting point is 914.5p, two-year-forward EPS of about 37p and a multiple of 24.5x.

To end-2027 (31-Dec-27, about 14 months away), the shares are worth about 925-1,060p. Two-year-forward EPS rises to about 42p (the FY2028-29 blend), an earnings leg of +13.5%. The multiple moves from 24.5x to 22-25x, a leg of −10% to +2%. Dividends paid inside the window, the FY2026 final and the FY2027 interim, are about 18-25p, or +2 to +3%. At the 38.8x guideline on the same EPS the shares would be worth about 1,630p (+78%, about +80% with dividends).

To mid-2029 (30-Jun-29), the shares are worth about 1,100-1,250p, a return of 9-14% a year, roughly the EPS compounding rate. Two-year-forward EPS rises to about 50p, an earnings leg of +35%; the multiple leg is again −10% to +2%; and dividends of about 60p add 6-7%.

The bull case needs consensus earnings, and the bear case needs only a cost year and a destocking half. Consensus two-year-forward EPS of about 52p at end-2027 gives 1,150-1,310p at our fair multiple (+29% to +46%), and about 1,450-1,560p (+60-70%) at 28-30x on evidence of upgrades. The bear case, 16x on about 36p, gives about 580p (−37%).

Earnings growth of 12-13% a year drives the return. EPS grows about 13% a year on our base to end-2027 and about 12% a year to mid-2029, because the royalty roughly triples (from £8.2m to £27m by FY2028), cost removal of £10-12m arrives at the US joint operation, the Rest of Group margin rises by less than a point, and buybacks of £30m a year add 1-2% a year net of interest forgone. Dividends add 2-3% a year at a 2% yield.

The multiple contributes nothing in our base, and becomes the swing factor only on upgrades or on a stall. The current phase (turning up, forecasts uncertain, no record of upgrades) does not earn the top of the range. Upgrades would take the multiple toward 28-30x, worth +15-20%; a stall would take it toward 16-18x, worth −25-35%.

The model summary's +54.8% return is mostly a re-rating to the guideline multiple applied to understated EPS, so this memo does not use it. At its 18-month column (31-Dec-27) the summary shows +54.8%: dividends +3.3%, the multiple +27.2% (from 30.5x today to the 38.8x guideline) and earnings +19.2%. At its three-year column (30-Jun-29) it shows +78.3%: dividends +5.4%, the multiple +27.2% and earnings +36.0%. Both drivers are artefacts. The starting multiple of 30.5x divides 926p by a two-year-forward EPS that the revenue-base error understates (about 30p, against about 37p with the inputs applied correctly), and the multiple leg assumes the 38.8x guideline. Corrected for the revenue base alone, the same guideline would produce an even larger re-rating leg (from 24.5x to 38.8x is +58%), which shows most clearly that the guideline multiple, not the earnings, is doing the work.

Where we differ from the market

The 20% gap on FY2028 EPS explains the whole difference between consensus's implied return of +29% to +46% at our fair multiple and our +4% to +19%. That gap sits in the US revenue line, the FY2028 Rest of Group margin, US marketing and interest income. Against the model summary's +54.8%, the difference is the multiple leg.

Strongest counter-case. The multiple leg could be the largest positive. At a decade-low multiple and with a floor under earnings, a single credible upgrade event (floor disclosure, a levy win, a post-anniversary scanner print above 15%) could take the stock from 24.5x to 28-30x on our EPS, worth +15-20% on top of the earnings leg; and the standstill expiry puts a bid option inside the three-year column.

What would change my view. Two consecutive upgrade events; disclosure of the royalty schedule; a sector re-rating with estimate support; a corrected model run showing the return at 22-25x.

Conclusion: on our base and at a 22-25x fair multiple, the total return is about +4% to +19% to end-2027 and +27% to +43% to mid-2029 (9-14% a year), driven by earnings growth of 12-13% a year and a 2% dividend yield, with the multiple roughly flat. The model summary's +54.8% and +78.3% are a 27% re-rating to a guideline multiple applied to understated EPS, and the bull case (+29% to +46% at our multiple) needs consensus earnings.
Score 44Score: 44, set by the Rater. The central base return of about +11% is earnings and dividends with the multiple flat, but weighting in a bear that needs only a cost year against a bull that needs consensus earnings pulls it to about +7-8%, inside the 0-10% D band at about 43 on the scale; the supportive three-year check (9-14% a year, earnings-led) lifts it a point, and the fat lower tail (-37%) keeps it off the top of the band.

The judgements that move the shares most, with the arithmetic

Four judgements each move EPS by 6-12%; the fifth, US revenue growth, barely moves EPS but moves the share price most. Base: FY2027 EPS 33.0p on 107.9m average shares; FY2028 EPS 39.3p on 105.3m shares; 25% tax; each £1m of EBITDA is worth about 0.70p (FY2027) or 0.71p (FY2028) of EPS.

1. The 2027-28 royalty step is the largest single unknown; it is contractual, and it is the item most likely to be disclosed or inferred first (in the segment EBITDA on 30-Mar-27). Our base has US EBITDA of £20.0m in FY2027 and £27.0m in FY2028. If the 2027 step is £24m, toward Deutsche Bank's path, EBITDA rises £4.0m, net income £3.0m and EPS 2.8p, to 35.8p (+8.5%). If the step is £17m, EBITDA falls £3.0m and EPS 2.1p, to 30.9p (−6%). An FY2028 royalty of £23m or £31m moves EBITDA by ±£4m and EPS by ±2.85p, to 36.4p or 42.1p (±7%). The step also shapes the FY2027 outlook: a company that knows its 2027 royalty is £24m would be more willing to endorse £63m of EBITDA.

2. Nothing truncates the downside to the Rest of Group margin in the hedge roll-off years. Rest of Group revenue is £258m in FY2027 and £266m in FY2028, so 1 point of margin is £2.6-2.7m of EBITDA, or 1.8-1.9p of EPS (about 5%). A 2027 pass-through of gas costs on the unhedged third, at forwards of €80/MWh, costs 0.5-1.0 points, or 0.9-1.8p, taking FY2027 EPS to 31.2-32.1p. A 2022-type move on the unhedged two-thirds in 2028 costs 1.5-2.5 points, or £4.0-6.7m of EBITDA and 2.9-4.8p of EPS, taking FY2028 EPS to 34.5-36.4p (−7% to −12%). The reverse, with gas at the €49/MWh forward for 2028 and prices catching up, adds 0.5-1.0 points, or 0.9-1.9p.

3. The US marketing judgement is correlated with the US growth judgement, and that correlation is the catch. Our base cuts US marketing from 20% to about 15% of US revenue in 2028, worth about £4m to Fevertree. If spend stays at 20% (Deutsche Bank's warning, and Redburn's own downside), EBITDA falls £4m and EPS 2.85p, to 36.4p in FY2028 (−7%). If spend falls to 11% (Redburn's base), EPS rises 2.85p, to 42.1p (+7%). The only branch that reaches consensus is the one in which marketing is cut and velocity holds; the branch in which marketing is cut and velocity falls hurts the multiple by more than the £4m.

4. US revenue growth is the most watched line, the least relevant to earnings and the most relevant to the share price. Our base has US growth of +12% in FY2027 and +10% in FY2028. Five points of FY2027 growth equal £8.2m of revenue, which at a half-share of a 15-20% incremental joint-operation margin is £0.6-0.8m of EBITDA, or 0.5p of EPS, and nothing while the floor binds. The share-price effect is large. A scanner growth rate below 10% before the April anniversary, with a destocking half, would in my estimate take the multiple from 24.5x toward 16-18x on about 37p, or 590-670p (−27% to −35%). A rate above 15% through the anniversary would hold 18% US growth in consensus and could take the multiple toward 28-30x on consensus's 52p at end-2027, or 1,450-1,560p (+60% to +70%).

5. The levy ruling is one-sided against our base: a loss changes nothing, and a win adds about 6% to FY2027 EPS. Our base carries about £3m a year of levy cost. A win removes that cost (+2.1p, +6% of FY2027 EPS) and reverses £5.4m once (about 3.8p, probably classed as exceptional). A related below-the-line item is also one-sided: consensus has pre-tax profit exceeding EBIT by £2.7m and £3.9m in FY2027-28, against our £1.4m and £1.3m. That difference is 0.9p and 1.9p of EPS, which consensus must lose unless the company stops buying back shares to keep the interest income.

13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

A dated watch-list with a real floor, not yet a live upgrade engine.

Fevertree is a reference premium brand whose economics are shared by design with bars, distributors and now a partner. The company has rebuilt its earnings model around a floored US royalty, exited its lowest-return activity, hedged its costs through 2027 and started returning real cash. That is strong, executed corporate change. But Molson Coors resources the change, a contract nobody outside the two companies can see transmits it to earnings, and it arrives into an environment that gives the category no growth, squeezes the UK consumer, taxes glass and will reprice glass energy in 2027-28.

Our base case is a credible recovery, but it sits 15-20% below a consensus that needs three undemonstrated levers to work together in FY2028. Our base has a 15% margin and EPS of 33p and 39p in FY2027-28. The operating-line revisions are already drifting toward our base, while the Buy share rises away from it.

The floor makes the next 18 months' profit unusually predictable for a stock this volatile. The same floor means that the US scanner print, which moves the share price monthly, cannot move profit in either direction until the joint operation's profit climbs above the floor.

At 24.5x our two-year-forward EPS the shares sit inside a 22-25x fair range for a turning-up stock, so the return is earnings and dividends. The total return is +4% to +19% to end-2027, with the multiple roughly flat, and about 9-14% a year to mid-2029.

The skew that Richard's test asks for, unusually positive odds of upgrades, is not present now and depends on dated events. It could appear at the Molson Coors call on 5-Nov-26, the January pre-close, the FY2027 outlook on 30-Mar-27, the April 2027 campaign anniversary or the February 2028 standstill expiry. Disclosure of the floor, a levy win or a post-anniversary scanner growth rate above 15% would make it appear.

Unpriced positives protect the downside

  • The floor covers the US glass slip
  • The free-cash-flow floor is realistic
  • The sugar threshold is a non-issue
  • The standstill expiry is a bid option

Unpriced negatives cap the next 18 months

  • The floor caps the US upside
  • 2027 glass energy
  • Marketing funds both growth and margin
  • Consensus counts the cash twice
Thesis's Change Forces' Strength68

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 68, set by the Rater. A strong, executed internal rebuild (topic 2, 68) reaches profits surely because the royalty is contractually floored, and drives EPS about 16% a year (topic 6, A at 90), but it touches only the US third of the business, recovers from a depressed base to a margin half its past level, and sits in a slightly net-negative environment (topic 1, 44). That is a clear positive change with one weaker part, high in the band below 75 rather than in it.

Foundations' Robustness48

Foundations' Robustness: 50, set by the Rater. A leading brand in a concentrated premium tier, capital-light with net cash (topic 3, 54), but not a stable or predictable franchise: margins collapsed from 30% to 8% in 2019-23 and sit at the 24th percentile, rent is shared with the trade and one partner, and the delivery record has no raise since 2022 (topic 4, 33). Unlike CVS its margins are neither stable nor protected by pricing power, and it lacks Judges Scientific's cash conversion, so it sits at typical.

Setups' Fit/Crispness38

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 58, set by the Rater. In substance the case is a Big Corporate Change-driven EPS upgrader: a large, executed pivot (the licence and floored royalty, portfolio, buybacks) produces an EPS step-up of about 18% a year to FY2028, and that part fits cleanly. One important element is loose and current problems blur it: the change is partner-executed and its transmission undisclosed, the floor caps how much US growth reaches earnings, and European share loss, the partner's own upheaval and rising central costs are problems today; whether consensus already holds the step-up is left to topics 7 and 12.

Case Riskiness46

Case Riskiness: 46, set by the Rater. Few drivers, a contractual EBITDA floor, hedges through 2027 and net cash constrain earnings risk, and the multiple is low in its own range, but the largest driver is an undisclosed contract, risk concentrates in one partner, one founder and unhedged 2027-28 energy, and a multiple still paid for a growth story can fall 25-35% (topic 9, 45). That is more than paper cuts, so a shade riskier than typical, a point above topic 9 for the low position in its own range.

A note on the model of record. The one-page model summary applied the forecast inputs to FactSet's statutory FY2025 revenue (£325.0m) instead of the brand revenue (£375.3m) on which the inputs were written. Every revenue and EBITDA line in the summary is therefore 13.4% too low and every EPS figure 17-20% too low, so its comparisons with consensus and its valuation (30.5x; a +54.8% eighteen-month return) are not usable. This memo uses the Analyst's cross-check figures, which are the inputs applied correctly; no input is changed. The Financial Analyst should replace the FY2025 revenue base of £325.0m with brand revenue of £375.3m (half-years £171.6m and £203.7m, and £183.6m for H1 2026), deduct the exceptional cash costs of £3.0m, £1.5m, £1.0m, £0.5m and £0.5m, and re-run the multiple and the total-return split on the corrected EPS, showing the return at 22-25x as well as at the 38.8x guideline.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
